chunks.text:
Andrian Than — software engineer building LLM agents for real users.

I'm a computer science student at San Jose State (3.7 GPA, graduating Spring 2027) who builds LLM agents for real users: copilots grounded in data, tested against golden sets, and shipped with the infrastructure to keep them honest.

I've also mentored 30+ people on working with AI coding tools like Cursor and Claude Code, including how to review and verify AI-generated changes.

Outside of engineering I lead in Alpha Kappa Psi and Spartan Analytics.

chunks.title: Blue Dome Technologies
chunks.text:
A chatbot I built that answers analysts' labeling questions from the written guidelines, using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with vector embeddings.
Problem

Analysts hit edge cases the guide doesn't make obvious, such as a partly hidden sign or a faded marking, and had to dig through a long document or ask a lead. That slows reviews and leads to inconsistent calls. Interview studies of annotation teams name ambiguous guidelines and edge cases among the main causes of inconsistent labels.
What it does

An analyst asks an edge-case question ("does a partially hidden sign still count?") and gets an answer grounded in the guideline text, with the source clause.
Architecture

A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline in two parts.

 
 
 
 INDEXING (AHEAD OF TIME) ANSWERING (PER QUESTION) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Guidelines documents (S3) 
 Chunker clauses, sections 
 Embedding model text to vectors 
 Vector store chunks + metadata 
 Analyst question in the review tool 
 Embed + retrieve top matching chunks 
 LLM answers from chunks 
 Answer cites the clause 
 no relevant chunk found: say so, flag the gap for a guideline update 
 
 
 Guideline chatbot architecture 
Indexing, ahead of time: guideline documents are split into chunks, embedded as vectors and stored with their clause ids.
Answering, per question: the question is embedded, the closest chunks are retrieved, and the model writes an answer from only those chunks and cites the clause.
No match: when nothing relevant is retrieved, the chatbot says so instead of guessing, and the gap can be flagged for a guideline update.
Impact
Questions answered per week: about 60
Answers with a cited clause: about 9 in 10
Accuracy on a hand-checked test set: about 85%
"Ask a lead" interruptions: about 15 a week before, about 5 after
Answer time: about 3 seconds

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser: a made-up guide, keyword plus local LSA vector retrieval, and templated answers that quote and cite the matching clause. It shows the shape of the feature, not the production system.

chunks.title: Blue Dome Technologies
chunks.text:
A search tool over the labeled road-scene images that finds images by description, finds images similar to one you pick, and flags near-duplicates, using CLIP-style image and text embeddings.
Problem

Finding more examples of an edge case meant paging through image folders, and repeated scenes got reviewed more than once, which wasted analyst time and skewed the training data.
What it does
Search by text: type a description like "faded lane marking at night" and get matching road scenes.
Similar images: pick an image and see its nearest neighbors, to find more examples of an edge case.
Near-duplicates: flag images that are almost identical, so analysts don't review the same scene twice and training data isn't skewed.
Architecture

Every image is turned into a vector once, and all three features read from the same index.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Images files in S3 
 Image encoder image to vector 
 Vector index vectors + metadata 
 Text query a scene in words 
 Text encoder same space as images 
 Ranked images closest by meaning 
 Picked image an analyst clicks one 
 Look up its vector already indexed 
 Nearest neighbors more of the edge case 
 Scheduled job checks the whole set 
 Read all vectors compare close pairs 
 Duplicate groups flagged for review 
 
 
 Image search architecture 
Indexing: an image encoder turns each image in S3 into a vector, stored in a vector index with the image's metadata.
Search by text: a text encoder maps the query into the same space as the images, and the closest images are ranked.
Similar images: a picked image's stored vector finds its nearest neighbors.
Duplicates: a scheduled job compares vectors and groups images above a similarity threshold, so analysts review one image per group.
Impact
Time to find examples of an edge case: about 20 minutes before, about 1 minute after
Search quality on test queries: about 8 in 10 of the top 5 results relevant
Images in the index: about 25,000
Near-duplicates found: about 1,800, roughly 7% of the set
Repeat review avoided: about 8 hours (1,800 images at about 15 seconds each)

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser: a made-up set of 27 scenes and a small hand-built attribute space instead of CLIP. Search, nearest neighbors and the duplicate threshold are real logic over that space. It shows the shape of the feature, not the production system.

chunks.title: Blue Dome Technologies
chunks.text:
A human-in-the-loop tool for QA analysts who verify AI-labeled roadway-infrastructure images. I wrote the design spec and built the prototype and the production-ready version.
Problem

The QA analysts who checked AI-labeled roadway images were already using an early prototype of the tool. They found it slow and hard to use. Likely causes: too many clicks per image, no keyboard shortcuts, no clear progress or undo.
Design spec

I wrote the design spec for the production version, then built it.
Architecture

As shipped. A Python Flask backend, a JavaScript frontend and a SQLite database for metadata, with images stored in S3. Analysts review each AI-labeled image and validate it, and TPM 2.0-backed authentication ties a login to a trusted device.

Target architecture. The same Flask API and frontend, with a managed Postgres in place of SQLite.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Browser JS review UI 
 Flask API TPM 2.0 device auth 
 Postgres labels, verdicts, users 
 S3 bucket image files 
 presigned upload (direct) 
 
 
 Target architecture 
The browser uploads images straight to S3 through presigned URLs, so large files never pass through Flask.
Flask records each image's S3 key, plus AI labels and analyst verdicts, in Postgres.
Device-trust authentication stays at the API.
Key decisions
Device trust: authentication is backed by TPM 2.0, so a login is tied to a trusted device.
Built across a 3-sprint roadmap with a product manager and a UI/UX designer, tracked in Trello, with updates to the founders.
Backend and data
Images live as files in an S3 bucket. The database holds each image's S3 key, and the viewer loads images by signed URL.
Metadata (images, AI labels, verdicts, users) lives in the database.
Why Postgres in the target: SQLite allows one writer at a time, and many analysts saving verdicts at once is its weakest case. Postgres adds concurrent writes, managed backups and filtered queries across labels, reviewers and status.
Impact
Time to review one image: about 45 seconds before, about 15 seconds after
Clicks per image: about 6 before, about 2 after
Analysts using it: about 8
Images reviewed per week: about 1,500
Delivered in: 3 sprints, with a product manager and a UI/UX designer

These figures are estimates, not measured results.

chunks.title: Hanna Center
chunks.text: Built in-house LLM tools with non-technical staff, including a grant-research agent that replaced an enterprise platform, avoiding $30k+ in vendor and subscription cost. Wrote the validation framework for agent accuracy, consistency, and safety.

chunks.title: Hanna Center
chunks.text:
An AI assistant that helps licensed clinicians write progress notes, and check notes they already wrote, against one behavioral-health payer's documentation standards. It expands a clinician's keywords into a note ready for the record, explains every decision, and rates notes pasted in.
Problem

Progress notes fail payer audits or supervisor review when they leave out the elements that show a session was medically necessary. Clinicians needed help writing notes that pass, and a way to learn what a strong note contains without a supervisor reading every one.
What it does
Start a new note: the clinician pastes keywords. The GPT lists everything that is missing in one message, then writes the note and an Expansion Breakdown that explains where each sentence came from and why.
Check a note: the clinician pastes an existing note in any format. The GPT rates it Tier 1, 2 or 3 and says exactly what to fix. It evaluates the note and does not rewrite it.
Stays honest: it never invents symptoms, diagnoses or client responses, and it never softens risk documentation.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Clinician new note, or check one 
 AI assistant instructions + rules 
 Output tier, note, breakdown 
 Knowledge base layered by authority: rules, guidance, guides, lookups 
 file search 
 
 
 Case note chatbot architecture 
One assistant with no backend code of its own. A single instructions file is the source of truth for the rules, the routing table and the output format.
The knowledge base is layered by authority: payer rules first, then audit guidance, sufficiency logic, supporting guides, and structured code and term lookups. When two layers disagree, the higher one wins.
The flow runs input, service type, a check of each of the three note sections, one message listing every gap, then the note and its breakdown.
Key decisions
No embellishment. Every sentence must trace to what the clinician said, because the note is a legal record. Gaps are flagged, not filled.
An authority hierarchy, so payer rules override generic advice.
Three tiers, with hard fails and soft suggestions kept apart. Missing administrative details are never graded.
Risk documentation in three proportional categories, not always required in full.
Telehealth checks are reminders only and never block a note.
A high-capability reasoning model is required, because smaller models loosen the ratings.
Impact
Rating: 3 tiers and 8 hard-fail conditions
Knowledge base: 15 files, including structured lookups of 259 diagnosis codes and 114 intervention terms
Rebuild: 15 to 20 minutes, with the smoke tests re-run after every instruction change

Estimated outcomes:
Time to write a progress note: about 15 minutes before, about 6 minutes after
Clinicians using it: about 12
Notes checked per week: about 50

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser. The real tool is an AI assistant configured with instructions and a knowledge base. The demo uses made-up documentation standards, rule checks for the eight conditions (two of them keyword heuristics), local retrieval for questions, and a note builder where every sentence comes from the input. It is not a language model, and it holds no real clinical content.

chunks.title: Hanna Center
chunks.text:
An agent that finds, scores and tracks grant opportunities for the organization, and replaced an enterprise grant platform. It scrapes funder sources every day, scores each new grant against criteria that staff edit, logs the good ones to a shared sheet, and emails a daily and a weekly digest.
Problem

Finding grants meant searching many funder websites by hand, and the paid platform that did it for us was expensive. The goal was a tool the team owned, that surfaced only grants worth a person's time, and whose scoring non-technical staff could change themselves.
What it does
Scrapes the funder sources every morning and removes duplicates.
Scores each new grant on a seven-flag framework, with a reason for every flag.
Logs grants above the sheet cutoff to a shared tracker where staff approve or skip them.
Emails a daily list of grants above the email cutoff, and a digest on Fridays.
Lets staff retune the scoring in plain English through a custom GPT, with a preview before any change.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Scheduler daily at 6 AM 
 Workflow fans out 
 Scrapers one per source 
 Processing filter, dedupe 
 Vector DB grants + vectors 
 Criteria doc editable by staff 
 Evaluator pre-filter, then score 
 Sheet + email tracker, daily, weekly 
 Editor preview, apply, undo 
 Custom GPT plain English 
 Staff non-technical 
 
 
 Grants agent architecture 
A scheduler starts the day's run. A workflow fans out to one scraper per source, and a processing step filters off-mission items, extracts details with an LLM, embeds them and writes them to a database with vector search.
The evaluator retrieves candidate grants by vector similarity, runs a cheap pre-filter model, then a stronger model scores the survivors against the criteria document.
Scores go to the sheet and the emails. The criteria live in a document that staff can edit, directly or through the custom GPT.
Key decisions
Criteria in a document, so non-technical staff change the scoring without code.
Preview, apply, undo for every edit made through the GPT: a change is previewed, applied with a one-time token that expires, and recorded so it can be reversed.
A cheap model first, a stronger model second, so most grants never reach the expensive step.
Server-side validation of every edit: whitelisted settings and checked values.
A managed scraping service instead of a headless browser, to keep the deployment light.
Impact
Vendor cost avoided: $30k+ across this tool and the incident tool below, replacing an enterprise grant platform and a paid add-on
Sources covered: 39, scraped every day at 6 AM and scored at 9 AM
Scoring: 7 flags and 6 department search profiles; the sheet shows grants scoring 5.0 and up, the email 6.0 and up
Running cost: about $16 to $19 a month, of which the LLM is about $2 to $5
Editing: staff change criteria in plain English, with preview and undo

Estimated outcomes:
Time spent finding grants: about 6 hours a week before, about 1 hour a week of review after
Grants a person reviews each week: about 40 before, about 10 after
Junk grants cut from the review pile: about 70%

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser: twelve made-up grants and funders, seven stand-in flags modeled on the shape of the real framework, and a deterministic scorer. The threshold, the digest and the tracker are live, and the Edit criteria tab runs a real preview, apply and undo with an expiring one-time token. Nothing here is real grant data.

chunks.title: Hanna Center
chunks.text:
A Microsoft Teams bot that lets residential-program staff file an incident report without leaving chat. Staff type a short command, fill a guided five-step form, and the bot creates the record in Salesforce for a supervisor to review. It replaced a paid add-on.
Problem

To file an incident report, staff had to log into Salesforce directly, which meant training, access and finding their way around a complex layout. Frontline staff needed a way to report from the tool they already had open.
What it does
Starts from a command typed in Teams, then walks through five short steps.
Fills in what it can: staff, youth and enrollment details come from lookups, so staff don't retype them.
Reviews before sending, with an edit button on every step.
Creates a Draft incident plus one linked record for each youth involved. A supervisor reviews and approves it in Salesforce.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Teams chat /ir and a form 
 Bot service routes messages 
 One function builds the record 
 Salesforce Draft incident 
 replies through the bot service, form state travels inside each card 
 
 
 Incident bot architecture 
Teams talks to a bot service, which calls one serverless function. The function validates the form, builds the incident and the linked youth records, and writes them to Salesforce.
Replies go back to Teams through the bot service. There is no database, queue or session store: the form's state travels inside each card, and nothing lives outside Salesforce.
Key decisions
One function, which keeps the infrastructure and the cost as small as possible.
State in the card, so the bot is stateless and a restart loses nothing.
Draft only: staff can create reports but not approve them, so a supervisor always reviews.
Dependent picklists with a rule that drops an invalid type and sub-type pair before anything is sent.
Adding a form field is a one-file change: the card input, the state key, the payload and the review card.
Impact
Vendor cost avoided: $30k+ across this tool and the grants agent above, which also replaced a paid add-on
Form: 5 steps, and a submit takes 1 to 3 seconds
Running cost: about $1 to $2 a month
Verification: a 54-check smoke test run after every deploy (53 passing, one transient), and 22 documented failure scenarios with fixes

Estimated outcomes:
Time to file an incident report: about 15 minutes in Salesforce directly, about 3 minutes in Teams
Staff using it: about 25
Reports filed per month: about 80

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser: a Teams-style chat, made-up youth and staff, and the same five-step flow. The dependent picklists, the review screen, the Draft record and the supervisor approval run real logic. Nothing here is real incident data.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text: Built Ask SDP, a tool-calling LLM copilot whose answers can't contain invented numbers, and shipped Forecast Lab, with Chronos-2 forecasts 32% better than baseline on backtest. Built the staging-to-prod pipeline behind 200+ staging deploys a week.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
Ask SDP is a tool-calling copilot over live consumption data: planners ask a question in plain language, and every number in the answer comes from a tool result, never from the model's imagination.
Problem

Demand planners were already asking an LLM questions about consumption data, and the answers read beautifully and were sometimes fiction. A confident invented number is worse than no answer: it flows into a planning decision, and nobody can tell afterwards which figures were real. The tooling the team had — dashboards and SQL — answered the questions accurately but slowly, one query at a time.
What it does
Answers only from tool results. An output rail extracts every number in a draft answer and checks each one against the tool results in the conversation. A figure with no source is stripped, and the answer ships without it.
Forces tool use where it matters. A code-gated routing floor sends data questions to a tool before the model can free-form an answer. On the routing evals that floor takes coverage to 35/35 metric intents with 0% free-route answers.
Grades metric understanding. Metric questions — error rates, deltas, forecast quality — grade 17/17 on the metric eval set.
Stops silent verdict flips. Every answer ends in a typed verdict stating what the data supports, so a conclusion cannot quietly change between runs.
Runs a sandboxed Python tool. Numeric questions go to a Python tool that accepts an allow-listed subset of the language and touches no network, returning a checked result into the conversation.
Architecture

The shape is a pipeline with one mandatory gate. A planner's question enters the routing floor; the floor decides whether the question needs data, and every data-bound path passes through a tool call before drafting. The draft then crosses the output rail, which verifies each figure against the tool results, and the answer leaves with a typed verdict.

The rail sits after the model rather than inside it because grounding is a checkable property, not a style the model can be prompted into. Putting the guarantee in code makes it testable in CI: a fabricated number either survives the rail or the build fails.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Planner's question 
 Routing floor code-gated 
 Python tool sandboxed 
 Data tool live consumption 
 Output rail every number checked 
 Typed verdict what the data supports 
 
 
 Ask SDP architecture 
The question hits the routing floor first; the floor is code, so a data question cannot reach the model ungated.
Tool calls run in parallel where a question needs more than one source.
The output rail re-reads the draft and the tool results together; any unmatched figure is removed before the answer ships.
The typed verdict closes the loop: the answer states its own grounding.
Key decisions
Grounding in code, not in the prompt. A prompt can ask the model to behave; a rail makes honesty the only way an answer ships. The cost is that every formatting change in the model's output has to keep parsing.
A routing floor instead of tool-choice. Leaving the choice to the model produced free-route answers on the evals; gating it in code took routing to 35/35 with 0% free-route answers. The cost is a hard boundary that occasionally routes a question a human would have answered from memory.
A typed verdict. A structured end-of-answer field makes a flipped conclusion visible and diffable. The cost is one more schema the prompts and evals must agree on.
A sandboxed Python tool with an AST allow-list. It lets the copilot compute rather than guess, while the allow-list and the no-network rule keep the blast radius of a bad generation near zero. The cost is maintenance: each accepted construct is a reviewed surface.
Strip, don't block. An unverifiable figure is removed and the rest of the answer ships, because a partial answer with only sourced numbers is more useful than an error page. The cost is answers that can be quieter than the question deserved.
Impact
Routing coverage 35/35 metric intents with 0% free-route answers.
Metric intents grade 17/17.
Grounding grades at micro-F1 0.854 against a 0.80 threshold.
No answer ships with a number that did not come from a tool result.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
The pipelines feed the app: weekly demand data lands in the analytics tables the planning app reads, and the same data rolls up into the executive reporting deck.
Problem

The executive deck was assembled by hand from queries that drifted between runs, and the analytics tables the app depended on went stale without anyone noticing — a planner investigating a demand spike could be reading last week's data and have no way to tell.
What it does
Builds the executive deck automatically. Weekly demand data flows into the 77-slide deck without a hand-assembled run, saving 20+ hours of reporting work each time.
Rebuilds on a schedule with verification. Each build of the analytics tables is checked before it is used: row counts and sanity checks run against the fresh build, not against hope.
Swaps atomically. A verified build replaces the live tables in one step, so a reader is never on a half-updated schema.
Polls freshness every 10 minutes. A staleness check runs continuously, so a broken upstream feed is an alert within minutes instead of a mystery next week.
Serves two consumers from one source. The planning app and the executive deck read the same verified tables, so a number quoted upstairs matches the number in the app.
Architecture

The source lands in a staging area; a freshness job polls it on a 10-minute interval, triggers a build, verifies the build, and swaps it in atomically. Downstream, two consumers read the swapped-in tables: the planning app and the executive deck.

Verification sits between build and swap because the dangerous failure is not a late table — that is visible — but a confidently wrong one, which only a check before the swap can catch.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Source weekly demand 
 Freshness 10-minute polling 
 Verified build checked rows 
 Atomic swap live tables 
 Planning app planners 
 Executive deck 77 slides 
 
 
 Data pipelines architecture 
The freshness job is the only thing that touches the source; consumers never read it directly.
A build that fails verification is discarded, and the previous tables keep serving.
The atomic swap is the whole freshness story: either the new tables are fully live or the old ones are.
Key decisions
Verify before swap, not after. A post-swap check catches a bad table after planners have already read it; a pre-swap check catches it while the cost is zero. The cost is holding the swap until verification finishes.
Atomic swap over in-place updates. Readers see one consistent generation of tables or the last good one, never a mixture. The cost is double storage during the swap window.
One source for app and deck. The number upstairs and the number in the app come from the same verified tables, which ends the "which number is right" argument. The cost is that the deck's format constrains the table shape.
A poll, not a push. Polling every 10 minutes makes staleness self-announcing with no upstream cooperation needed. The cost is up to 10 minutes of lag that a push-based design could have avoided.
Impact
Weekly demand data lands in the 77-slide executive deck automatically — 20+ hours of reporting work saved per run.
Automated freshness with verified builds, atomic swap, and 10-minute polling.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
The eval harness is the golden set that grades the copilot's routing, metric and grounding changes in CI, and the CI pipeline around it turned a push-straight-to-main team into one with staging, review and prod gates.
Problem

The copilot could regress silently: a prompt change that improved tone could quietly loosen grounding. At the same time the team pushed untested code straight to main, so the only test of a change was production, and the people affected were 10+ data analysts and demand planners doing real planning work on it.
What it does
Grades every change against a golden set. Routing, metric and grounding changes in CI are graded against a fixed set of questions with known-good answers, so a regression is a failed check rather than a surprise.
Runs a negative control. The set includes a fabricated number that must fail grounding: if a change lets the invented figure through, the run fails, by design.
Holds the line on grounding. Grounding grades at micro-F1 0.854 against a 0.80 threshold; a change that drops the grade is a revert, not a debate.
Gives the team staging. Every branch deploys to staging of its own, so a change is tried on real data before anyone reviews it.
Opens the draft PR for you. Pushing a branch auto-opens a draft pull request, which turned "put it up for review" from a chore into a side effect of pushing.
Deploys prod on merge. Merging to main is the only path to production, and it is the same pipeline every time.
Architecture

A pull request enters CI, CI runs the golden set, and the golden set feeds three gates — routing, metrics, grounding. A merge is only reachable when all three pass, and a negative control feeds the grounding gate so that a fabricated number fails the run by construction.

The gates are separate because they fail for different reasons: routing and metrics fail when behaviour changes, grounding fails when honesty does. One combined grade would let a routing win paper over a grounding loss.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Pull request in CI 
 Golden set graded questions 
 Routing gate tool coverage 
 Metrics gate intents 
 Grounding gate numbers checked 
 Negative control fabricated number 
 Merge all gates pass 
 
 
 Evals and CI architecture 
The golden set is versioned with the code that grades it, so a grade always means the same thing.
The negative control has failed real changes: when the output rail was being built, the control proved the gap the rail closed.
Staging and the draft PR are plumbing around the same pipeline, not a second one.
Key decisions
A golden set instead of spot checks. A fixed, versioned set makes a grade comparable across time, which is the whole point. The cost is maintaining the set as the product's behaviour grows.
A negative control on the grounding gate. A gate that has never failed proves nothing; the fabricated number makes the grounding gate falsifiable every run. The cost is one contrived question that reviewers have to accept as load-bearing.
Per-branch staging before review. Reviewers comment on behaviour they have actually clicked, not diffs they imagine. The cost is infrastructure: deploys for every branch, including the ones that go nowhere.
Auto-opened draft PRs. The pipeline produces the review artifact instead of relying on habit. The cost is a draft PR queue with more noise in it, which the team decided was the cheaper problem.
Prod on merge only. One path to production means one thing to watch. The cost is that hotfixes queue behind the same merge.
Impact
Routing, metrics and grounding changes grade in CI; grounding holds at micro-F1 0.854 against the 0.80 threshold, routing at 35/35 with 0% free-route answers, metrics at 17/17.
A fabricated number must fail the negative control, and does.
200+ staging deploys a week across 10+ data analysts and demand planners.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
Forecast Lab is the shipping vehicle for the forecasting work: Chronos-2 forecasts on a planner's watchlist, shaping controls for business knowledge, and a guarded write-back into the planning system.
Problem

The planning system's baseline forecasts were produced by a gradient-boosted model that handled seasonality but missed the shape the business could see coming. Planners corrected forecasts by hand, and the corrections lived in spreadsheets where nobody could grade them. Meanwhile two foundation-model forecasters had appeared that the team had never compared on its own data.
What it does
Compares models on real backtests. LightGBM, Chronos-2 and TimesFM run on the same history and are graded on the same error metric, so model choice is a measurement rather than a preference.
Puts the winner on a watchlist. Planners follow the series they care about and see Chronos-2 forecasts generated for each.
Lets planners shape a forecast. Where the business knows something the data does not — a launch, a holiday shift — a shaping control adjusts the forecast, and the adjustment is recorded as a diff.
Writes back only through the guarded path. A shaped forecast lands in the planning system through the interface the system already exposes, never as a silent mutation.
Keeps the baseline visible. The gradient-boosted baseline runs alongside, so an improvement is always relative to what the team had.
Architecture

The pipeline runs history through the candidate models, collects their errors, and hands the comparison to the watchlist service, which serves forecasts and records shaping. Write-back is a separate guarded step, so generation and mutation never share a path.

The separation matters because a forecast is cheap to regenerate and expensive to undo: anything that changes the planning system goes through the checked interface, and everything upstream of it can fail loudly without touching anyone's data.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Demand history 
 Baseline gradient boosted 
 Chronos-2 foundation model 
 Comparison same backtest 
 Watchlist forecast shaping 
 Guarded write-back to the planning system 
 
 
 Forecast Lab architecture 
History enters both model boxes unchanged, so the comparison is apples to apples.
The comparison step owns the error metric and publishes it; the watchlist never asserts an improvement the comparison did not measure.
Shaping is a recorded diff on top of a generated forecast, not an edit to the model.
The guarded write-back is the only arrow that reaches the planning system.
Key decisions
Grade models on the team's own backtest. Public benchmarks said the foundation models were good; the backtest said by how much on this data: lag-zero error fell from $17.0M to $11.6M, 32% better than baseline. The cost is maintaining a backtest harness nobody gets to skip.
Ship the comparison, not just the winner. Keeping the baseline visible keeps the improvement honest and gives the next model change its reference point. The cost is running two forecasters where one would do.
Shaping as a recorded diff. Planners' adjustments become data — gradable, revertible, and auditable — instead of invisible spreadsheet edits. The cost is that shaping has a schema, and "just change the number" is no longer a thing.
A guarded write-back path. Regeneration is cheap; wrong data in the planning system is not. The cost is a code review for every change to the write-back surface.
Impact
Lag-zero backtest error fell from $17.0M to $11.6M — 32% better than the baseline.
Forecast Lab shipped to planners: watchlist, Chronos-2 forecasts, forecast shaping, guarded write-back.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
The planning app is the React and FastAPI application planners live in, rebuilt internally around layers that keep the UI, the data access and the domain logic from tangling.
Problem

The app had grown screen-first: each feature reached directly into whatever data it needed, so a change in one screen broke another, and the data layer had three competing conventions. New engineers paired with planners on real work but hesitated to touch the app, because nothing told them where a change belonged. The visual state of 165 routes was held together by attention rather than by tooling.
What it does
Shares a component library. The screens that planners use every day are built from one library, so a pattern fixed once is fixed everywhere.
Routes through modules behind a thin entry point. Each route module owns its screen; the app entry point stays small enough to read in one sitting.
Reaches data through a data-client facade. Screens call domain modules through one facade, and the facade is the only place that knows how the data layer is reached.
Enforces the layers with lint guards. A screen that imports past the facade fails lint in the change that tries it, with a message pointing at the right layer.
Regression-tests the visuals. A harness screenshots 165 routes on every change and diffs them against the last accepted state.
Architecture

The browser talks to route modules; route modules compose shared components and call the data-client facade; the facade fronts the domain modules that own queries and writes. The domain systems sit behind that last layer.

The facade is deliberately the only path to data. One path means one place to add caching, one place to instrument, and one place a new engineer can read to learn what the app can do.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Browser planners 
 Route modules one per screen 
 Data-client facade the only path to data 
 Domain modules queries and writes 
 Domain systems behind the facade 
 
 
 Planning app architecture 
The three stacked layers are ordered: a route module may use components and the facade, never the domain systems directly.
The lint guards encode that order, so the architecture survives people who have not read this page.
The visual regression harness watches all 165 routes; a screenshot diff is part of every change.
Key decisions
A facade over a wider refactor. The data-client facade gave every screen one blessed path without rewriting them all at once; screens migrated as they were touched. The cost is a transition period where the old patterns still exist in older screens.
Lint guards instead of convention docs. A document is read once; a failing lint rule is read every time someone tries the wrong import. The cost is writing the rules and keeping their messages kind.
A visual regression harness before a component freeze. Locking down patterns without watching the 165 routes would have moved breakage into production. The cost is a snapshot store and a review step that occasionally catches trivia.
Route modules behind a thin entry. The app entry point stopped being the place where routes tangled, which made the app legible to new engineers. The cost is a little ceremony per route.
Impact
A shared component library, route modules behind a thin app entry point, and a data-client facade over the domain modules — with lint guards that enforce the layers.
A visual regression harness across 165 routes, run on every change.

The window below is a mock recreation of the work log I kept through the internship — the running notes I wrote for myself and the next person. It is a recreation: every name and identifier in it is invented, while the figures are the real, published ones from this page.
What it is

A work log is an engineer's running record: what shipped, what it cost, what broke, and what the next person needs to know. The real one is internal, so this window recreates its shape — headline result up top, one section per system, and a handbook for whoever comes next — with stand-in names and identifiers throughout.

The recreation exists because the organisation of the work is the interesting part. How the systems were graded, what each decision traded away, and what got written down for successors is the actual job; the sanitised names do not change that.
About the demo

The window runs the real selection and expansion logic — the same tab-and-row behaviour as every other demo on this site — over invented content. Every person, system name and identifier in it is invented; the impact metrics in it are the real, published figures from this page, checked against the same allowlist. Nothing in the window is confidential.
